rationale: bugs_open/006 §C. The `claimed-item-timeout` scheduled task is the fleet's only self-heal for a claim whose handler finished but whose `mark_complete` write was lost (pod death, or the lost child response of bugs_open/003). It has two branches: auto-complete on evidence at 15 minutes, and reset to 'triaged' at 40 minutes. The evidence branch is a hand-written artifact test PER item_type and only three exist (needs_content_page, page_rerender, needs_design), so the other fifteen item types fall through to reset EVEN WHEN THEIR WORK SUCCEEDED — which is exactly the churn §C was filed about. Measured live 2026-07-26 over 14 days of `error LIKE 'Claim timed out%'`: 84 timeouts against 14 auto-completions; needs_page (the item type in §C's own original symptom) had 27 timeouts and has NEVER been auto-completed; content_rewrite 15/0; needs_imagery 6/0. Eleven of those items ended 'failed' and one 'unresolved' — attempts exhausted on work that was already done. The bug file asks for the structural answer rather than fifteen more per-type branches: 'The structural fix this section asks for (complete atomically, or retry the completion write idempotently) is still the right one, and would make the per-item-type evidence branches unnecessary rather than needing fifteen more of them.' This change supplies the generic evidence those per-type tests are approximating. It does NOT attempt to fix why the write is lost — that is bugs_open/003's pod-death/lost-response question, whose F2+F3 are live in v1.0.1159 and owner-ratified; §C asked for a recovery layer that works for every item type, and that is the scope here. It is a scheduled_tasks pre_query change, so it is live immediately with no image roll.

plan.summary: Give the claim-timeout sweep ONE generic completion-evidence branch — the handler's own orchestration reaching COMPLETED after the claim — replacing the need for a hand-written artifact test per item_type, and pin the one place where parity with the normal completion path would be unsafe (item types whose Go verifier can block completion) with a lockstep test that reads the migration itself.

edits.symbol: scheduled_tasks.pre_query WHERE name='claimed-item-timeout' — new CTE completed_by_orchestration
edits.rationale: The evidence the three artifact branches reach for is already recorded in ONE place for EVERY item type: the handler orchestration row, which carries the work item id because both dispatch loops pass it through call_handler.input_mapping. Verified live before building, three ways. (1) Reach is 100/100 over a 6-hour window — deliberately shorter than orchestration_states retention (~2 days, measured: 1,819 of 1,840 rows are from the last 48h) so no purge confounds it: page_rerender 92/92, needs_page 3/3, needs_content_page 2/2, nav_drift 1/1, missing_adoption_tracker_page 1/1, missing_protocol_tracker_page 1/1. (2) The item types that resolve to NOTHING (needs_section_data 0/7, cta_names_unknown_destination, needs_experience_plan) are completed by paths that never claim, so they can never be in the 'claimed' status this sweep reads. (3) Only two agents claim at all, and the second uses a status this sweep never looks at. The standard is PARITY with the lost mark_complete write, not something stricter: the dispatch loop calls complete_work_item on a handler saga that reached its own complete_workflow, so reproducing that is correct and anything stricter would leave finished work re-running. `o.updated_at > wi.claimed_at` is what makes a re-claim safe — an orchestration from a previous attempt completed before the current claim was taken. The three artifact branches are RETAINED as the fallback for a claim whose orchestration row has already been purged. The new branch writes a DIFFERENT error marker from the artifact branch so its effect is measurable and cannot be confused with the branches that already existed.
edits.sketch:
WITH completed_by_orchestration AS (
    UPDATE site_work_items wi
    SET status = 'complete',
        completed_at = NOW(),
        error = 'Auto-completed: handler orchestration completed after claim'
    WHERE wi.status = 'claimed'
      AND wi.claimed_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '15 minutes'
      AND wi.item_type NOT IN ('truncated_component', 'hardcoded_section_colors', 'empty_section')
      AND EXISTS (
        SELECT 1 FROM orchestration_states o
        WHERE o.initial_request_data->'input_data'->>'work_item_id' = wi.id::text
          AND o.status = 'COMPLETED'
          AND o.updated_at > wi.claimed_at
      )
    RETURNING id, item_type, handler_agent, status
),
completed_by_evidence AS (   -- unchanged 3 artifact branches, now also excluding
    ...  AND wi.id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM completed_by_orchestration)  ...
),
reset AS (                   -- unchanged, now excluding both
    ...  AND id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM completed_by_orchestration)
         AND id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM completed_by_evidence)  ...
)

edits.symbol: migration guards 1-3 (row updated / PREPARE parses / real-pre_query probe pair)
edits.rationale: pre_query is a SQL string in a text column: NOTHING validates it at write time, the scheduler runs it every 120 seconds, and a syntax error there would silently kill the fleet's only claim self-heal while every surface still reads 'enabled, firing normally'. Guard 2 PREPAREs the stored string — parses and plans against the real schema without executing or touching a row. Guard 3 plants a positive and a negative probe and then EXECUTES THE REAL STORED pre_query, asserting on the resulting row status and marker — deliberately NOT a restatement of the predicate, because a check that shares the fix's own expression cannot falsify it (it would pass against a typo'd pre_query that never fires in production). The negative control is there because a green case alone cannot fail: without it the guard would pass just as happily against a branch that completes everything. All four assertions were fault-injected and watched to fail with the right diagnostic before being trusted (branch negated; branch widened to accept FAILED; RETURNING misspelled; new branch made to write the OLD marker). Probes are inserted and deleted inside the transaction, so they are never visible to another session and never survive the file.

The one place parity with the normal completion path would be UNSAFE. complete_work_item does not complete unconditionally — verifyBeforeComplete consults a per-item_type verifier that can BLOCK completion, which is the bugs_open/017 and /021 completion-lie guard. SQL cannot call a Go verifier, so the three item types that have one are excluded from the new branch and keep falling through to reset: strictly safer than parity, and free today because none of the three appears anywhere in the 14-day timeout data. But that makes the SQL exclusion list and the RegisterVerifier() calls one contract held in two places, and the drift is silent and one-sided: register a fourth verifier, leave the SQL alone, and the sweep auto-completes an item the verifier would have blocked, with no caller to notice because a sweep has none. The test reads the migration file and extracts its exclusion list rather than comparing against a third literal copy here, because a guard whose own copy can drift is not a guard. It asserts BOTH directions (registered-but-not-excluded, and excluded-but-not-registered) and fails loudly rather than silently if the migration is missing or the SQL was reshaped so the regex no longer matches. All three failure modes were fault-injected and watched to fail.

plan.risks: (1) PARITY, NOT STRICTNESS, IS THE DELIBERATE CHOICE. A handler saga can reach complete_workflow without fixing the defect — page-build-handler's complete_error path is a success-labelled complete_workflow, and that is what the verifier registry exists to catch. This branch will auto-complete such an item, exactly as the dispatch loop's own mark_complete would have. That is the intended standard: the sweep is recovery for a LOST WRITE, and a recovery that is stricter than the write it replaces leaves finished work re-running, which is the defect being fixed. The three item types where a verifier could have blocked completion are excluded, so the gap is no wider than it was before this change — for every other item type the alternative today is not a verifier, it is a redundant re-run. (2) LATE-HANDLER EDGE CASE, accepted and documented in the migration header: if a handler finishes AFTER its item was reset and re-claimed, its COMPLETED orchestration post-dates the NEW claimed_at, so the new claim auto-completes on the old handler's evidence and the second handler's run is abandoned. The work genuinely is done and this is strictly better than today, where both runs go to completion. (3) LOCKSTEP DRIFT is the residual risk and it is why the Go test reads the migration rather than a copy; the test cannot, however, catch someone editing the pre_query directly in the database instead of through a migration file — the same class as any config-in-DB change, and the reason guard 1 asserts the row actually carries the new branch. (4) PERFORMANCE is not a concern at current volume — a correlated EXISTS over orchestration_states (~1,840 rows, ~2 day retention) every 120 seconds — but there is no index on the JSON path, so if orchestration retention is ever lengthened substantially this should get an expression index. Stated rather than pre-optimised. (5) NOT IN (SELECT id FROM cte) is the idiom already used by the pre-existing reset branch, so the new CTE follows the file's own established pattern for excluding rows another data-modifying CTE already touched, rather than introducing a second convention. (6) SCOPE: this does not address WHY the completion write is lost. That is bugs_open/003's pod-death / lost-child-response question (F2+F3 live v1.0.1159, owner-ratified). §C asked for a recovery layer covering every item type and that is what is delivered; the boundary is stated in the bug file rather than implied.
